scenes.visual: Title card 'Fifteen to Eight' over a cartoon rocky shore with an ORANGE sea star. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: TEAL (#0e7c86) = prey; ORANGE (#e57200) = predators; dark ink = the orbit and labels; grey neutrals for other species. Symbols on screen exactly as in the lesson: N (prey), P (predators), N*, P*, r, a, e, m. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Animals and ledgers are simple cartoons labelled 'schematic'; phase-plane orbits and time series are computed from the Lotka-Volterra model with the lesson's worked numbers (r = 1, a = 0.01, e = 0.1, m = 0.5) and labelled 'computed'. In this film: mussels are TEAL (the dominant prey); Pisaster is ORANGE; barnacles, algae, chitons and limpets are distinct grey-neutral tiles. Rock-tile grids are schematic, not Paine's data; only the counts 15 and 8 are from his 1966 paper.

scenes.tts: The first film showed each kill entered in two ledgers. Now follow the kills one link further, to the species the prey compete with.
scenes.visual: A brief recap: the two ledgers from the first film, TEAL and ORANGE, linked by the chain. A third grey ledger slides in beside the TEAL one, labelled 'species the prey compete with', and a dotted arrow runs from ORANGE through TEAL to grey.
scenes.narration: The first film showed each kill entered in two ledgers. Now follow the kills one link further, to the species the prey compete with.

scenes.tts: You might expect every species a predator eats to do better without it. So what happens to a rocky shore when its sea star is gone?
scenes.visual: A rocky shore at low tide. An ORANGE sea star is lifted off the rock by a hand. A question mark over the shore; small grey and TEAL tiles wait on the rock.
scenes.narration: You might expect every species a predator eats to do better without it. So what happens to a rocky shore when its sea star is gone?

scenes.tts: On this rocky shore, space on the rock is a limiting resource: its supply caps the populations that use it. Mussels are the strongest competitors for that space.
scenes.caption: On this rocky shore, space on the rock is a limiting resource: its supply caps the populations that use it. Mussels are the strongest competitors for that space.
scenes.visual: A square of rock drawn as a tile grid, mixed tiles of barnacles, algae, chitons and limpets (grey neutrals) with some TEAL mussel tiles. The grid's edge glows, labelled 'limiting resource: space on the rock'. TEAL mussel tiles pulse, labelled 'strongest competitors for space'.
scenes.narration: On this rocky shore, space on the rock is a limiting resource: its supply caps the populations that use it. Mussels are the strongest competitors for that space.

scenes.tts: The sea star pie-sass-ter oh-kray-shus eats mussels. It also eats barnacles, chitons, limpets and snails. Follow the orange arrows to each of its prey.
scenes.caption: The sea star Pisaster ochraceus eats mussels. It also eats barnacles, chitons, limpets and snails. Follow the orange arrows to each of its prey.
scenes.visual: The ORANGE sea star labelled 'Pisaster ochraceus' moves over the grid. Thin ORANGE arrows point to each prey type in turn as named: TEAL mussels, then grey barnacles, chitons, limpets and snails.
scenes.narration: The sea star Pisaster ochraceus eats mussels. It also eats barnacles, chitons, limpets and snails. Follow the orange arrows to each of its prey.

scenes.tts: In the early nineteen sixties, Robert Paine began keeping pie-sass-ter off one patch of shore at Mukkaw Bay, Washington. He left a neighbouring stretch alone as a control, and surveyed both along line transects.
scenes.caption: In the early 1960s, Robert Paine began keeping Pisaster off one patch of shore at Mukkaw Bay, Washington. He left a neighbouring stretch alone as a control, and surveyed both along line transects.
scenes.visual: A map pin 'Mukkaw Bay, Washington; removal began early 1960s'. Two tile grids side by side, labelled 'adjacent control' and 'removal patch'. A hand flicks ORANGE sea stars off the removal grid. Dashed lines across both grids labelled 'line transects'. A counter above the removal patch only: 'species on the rock: 15'.
scenes.narration: In the early 1960s, Robert Paine began keeping Pisaster off one patch of shore at Mukkaw Bay, Washington. He left a neighbouring stretch alone as a control, and surveyed both along line transects.

scenes.tts: The predator is gone from the patch. Will the number of species holding space on the rock go up, or down?
scenes.visual: Both grids frozen. Over the removal patch, two tags: 'up?' and 'down?'. The counter reads 15.
scenes.narration: The predator is gone from the patch. Will the number of species holding space on the rock go up, or down?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; a 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: species on the rock, up or down?'.

scenes.tts: Down. By his nineteen sixty six report, the removal patch held eight species on the rock instead of fifteen. The control did not lose species in the same way.
scenes.caption: Down. By his 1966 report, the removal patch held 8 species on the rock instead of 15. The control did not lose species in the same way.
scenes.visual: Time runs on the removal grid only; its counter falls from 15 to 8 (on screen: '15 → 8, Paine 1966'). The control grid stays mixed; its counter reads 'no comparable loss'. Small tag: 'grids schematic; counts from Paine 1966'.
scenes.narration: Down. By his 1966 report, the removal patch held 8 species on the rock instead of 15. The control did not lose species in the same way.

scenes.tts: Here is how the patch filled. Acorn barnacles settled first and took most of the open rock. Then small mussels and gooseneck barnacles crowded them out. Algae lost their space.
scenes.visual: Replay of the removal grid, slower: grey acorn-barnacle tiles spread over open rock ('within months'); then TEAL mussel tiles and grey gooseneck-barnacle tiles push in tile by tile, crowding the acorn barnacles; algae tiles flicker out. Label 'schematic sequence'.
scenes.narration: Here is how the patch filled. Acorn barnacles settled first and took most of the open rock. Then small mussels and gooseneck barnacles crowded them out. Algae lost their space.

scenes.tts: With pie-sass-ter eating mussels, space kept opening for weaker competitors. Without it, mussels took the rock. The sea star raised richness by freeing space, not by eating species that harmed the rest.
scenes.caption: With Pisaster eating mussels, space kept opening for weaker competitors. Without it, mussels took the rock. The sea star raised richness by freeing space, not by eating species that harmed the rest.
scenes.visual: Split view: on the control grid an ORANGE sea star removes a TEAL mussel tile and a grey tile settles into the gap; on the removal grid TEAL mussels cover almost every tile. Label 'richness = number of species on the rock'.
scenes.narration: With Pisaster eating mussels, space kept opening for weaker competitors. Without it, mussels took the rock. The sea star raised richness by freeing space, not by eating species that harmed the rest.

scenes.tts: Now look at one chiton. pie-sass-ter eats chitons, so the sea star costs it some lives. But the sea star also keeps mussels off the rock, which keeps the chitons' space and food.
scenes.caption: Now look at one chiton. Pisaster eats chitons, so the sea star costs it some lives. But the sea star also keeps mussels off the rock, which keeps the chitons' space and food.
scenes.visual: Zoom on a single grey chiton tile. An ORANGE arrow from the sea star to the chiton with a minus sign, labelled 'direct: eaten'. Then a longer route: ORANGE arrow to TEAL mussels (minus), TEAL arrow to the chiton's rock space and food (minus), net shown as a grey plus arrow to the chiton, labelled 'indirect: space and food freed from mussels'.
scenes.narration: Now look at one chiton. Pisaster eats chitons, so the sea star costs it some lives. But the sea star also keeps mussels off the rock, which keeps the chitons' space and food.

scenes.tts: Two arrows, with opposite signs. Without the sea star, chitons left the patch for lack of space and food. So here, the sea star's indirect help to some of its own prey outweighed what it ate.
scenes.visual: The two arrows side by side: small ORANGE minus 'direct', larger grey plus 'indirect'. On the removal grid, chiton tiles slide off the rock, tagged 'left: lack of space and food'. Caption on screen: 'net effect = direct + indirect (in this patch)'.
scenes.narration: Two arrows, with opposite signs. Without the sea star, chitons left the patch for lack of space and food. So here, the sea star's indirect help to some of its own prey outweighed what it ate.

scenes.tts: In a short note three years after his report, Paine used the word keystone. A keystone species has an effect on its community that is large relative to its abundance.
scenes.visual: A stone arch; a small wedge at the top lights up ORANGE labelled 'keystone (Paine, 1969, per the PNAS memorial)'. The arch's large blocks are labelled 'abundance', the wedge 'effect'. On screen: 'keystone species: effect large relative to abundance'.
scenes.narration: In a short note three years after his report, Paine used the word keystone. A keystone species has an effect on its community that is large relative to its abundance.

scenes.tts: Eating the dominant competitor, and so helping weaker ones, is called keystone predation. But this was one removal patch and one control. It was a strong local result, not yet a general law.
scenes.visual: Label 'keystone predation: eat the dominant competitor, weaker ones gain'. The two grids shrink to one pair with a tag 'n = 1 removal, 1 control'. A faint map of the coast with many unknown shores marked '?'.
scenes.narration: Eating the dominant competitor, and so helping weaker ones, is called keystone predation. But this was one removal patch and one control. It was a strong local result, not yet a general law.

scenes.tts: So a predator's effects can run through the species it eats, to the species they compete with. On Paine's shore, they did.
scenes.visual: The three ledgers from the opening, ORANGE to TEAL to grey, with the dotted arrow now solid, running through the TEAL mussel ledger to the grey ledgers of barnacles, algae and chitons. Small tag: 'Paine's shore; size and sign vary by community'.
scenes.narration: So a predator's effects can run through the species it eats, to the species they compete with. On Paine's shore, they did.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'A predator's effects can run through the species it eats.'
